title: Politics
author: Aristotle
openingChapterLabel: Book I — The Polis and Its Origins
openingText: Every state is a community of some kind, and every community is established with a view to some good; for mankind always act in order to obtain that which they think good. But, if all communities aim at some good, the state or political community, which is the highest of all, and which embraces all the rest, aims, and in a greater degree than any other, at the highest good. Hence it is evident that the state is a creation of nature, and that man is by nature a political animal. And he who by nature and not by mere accident is without a state, is either above humanity, or below it.
about:
Aristotle's Politics is a treatise on the nature of the political community — what cities are for, what kinds of regimes are possible, what makes a citizen, what role wealth and virtue play in public life. It is the second half of Aristotle's practical philosophy; the Nicomachean Ethics is the first. Together they argue that the good for individuals can only be fully realized in a well-ordered polis.

Aristotle wrote it in Athens in the 4th century BCE, drawing on a survey of 158 different Greek constitutions (most lost). It is more empirical than Plato's Republic — Aristotle starts from what cities actually look like and reasons from there. The book founded political science as a discipline and remains the indispensable starting point for thinking about political life.

angleCards.title: The polis as natural.
angleCards.text: Aristotle's claim that man is by nature a political animal — that the state is not a convention we invented but the completion of our nature — is one of the most consequential ideas in the Western tradition. It shapes what he thinks citizenship means, what it means to live well, and why political philosophy matters at all.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to follow Aristotle's argument that the polis is not a human invention but a natural end — and test whether that claim holds up, what it demands of citizens, and what it rules out.

angleCards.title: Why constitutions fall.
angleCards.text: Book V is the most modern part of the Politics: a systematic analysis of revolution, factional conflict, and regime decay. Aristotle catalogs the specific grievances, misjudgments, and structural flaws that bring down oligarchies and democracies — and what rulers can do to slow the process. The patterns he identifies recur across 2,400 years of political history.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read the Politics primarily through Book V — Aristotle's analysis of why regimes collapse, what triggers stasis, and whether his account of political decay still explains what we see in the world today.

angleCards.title: The middle-class state.
angleCards.text: Aristotle argues that the most stable constitution is one in which the middle class is large and dominant — neither extreme poverty nor extreme wealth, because both produce instability and faction. This is not a sentimental claim. It is an empirical observation drawn from 158 constitutions. His argument for polity as the best practical regime rests entirely on it.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to trace Aristotle's argument that political stability depends on the size and character of the middle class — and ask whether his empirical case holds, and what it implies for how we think about inequality today.

angleCards.title: Citizenship: who belongs?
angleCards.text: Book III opens with a question that has never been fully settled: who is a citizen? Aristotle's answer — someone who shares in deliberation and judgment — seems simple, but its implications are enormous. It excludes slaves, women, mechanics, and resident aliens. Wrestling with where he draws the line, and why, is the only honest way to read his political theory.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to follow Aristotle's definition of citizenship in Book III — who qualifies, who is excluded, and on what grounds — and use that definition as a lens for evaluating the rest of his political argument.

cast.name: The Polis
cast.description: Not merely a city or a state but the highest form of human association — the community that makes the good life possible. Aristotle argues the polis is natural, not conventional: it is the telos toward which family and village are always moving. Without it, a human being cannot fully be what a human being is.

cast.name: Polity (Politeia)
cast.description: Aristotle's name for the mixed constitution that blends democracy and oligarchy around a dominant middle class. Not ideal in the abstract — that is aristocracy or kingship — but the best a real city can realistically achieve. Most of his constitutional recommendations in Books IV–VI are aimed at helping cities approximate it.

cast.name: The Citizen
cast.description: Defined in Book III as one who shares in deliberation and judgment — who rules and is ruled in turn. Aristotle's definition excludes slaves, women, artisans, and resident aliens, and he knows that different constitutions produce different answers. The question of who counts as a citizen is the hinge on which everything else turns.

cast.name: Revolution (Stasis)
cast.description: Book V's subject: factional conflict, coup, and constitutional breakdown. Aristotle analyses the specific triggers — perceived injustice, extreme inequality, personal ambition, ethnic and economic division — that destabilise each constitution type. His taxonomy of how democracies slide into demagogy and oligarchies into faction is still used by political scientists.

cast.name: The Middle Class
cast.description: Aristotle's most practical political insight: constitutions held together by a large, prosperous middle class are the most stable and the least prone to revolution. Extreme wealth and extreme poverty both generate instability — the one through arrogance, the other through resentment. Polity is the regime that makes the middle class its governing principle.

cast.name: Slavery and Household
cast.description: Book I grounds political life in the household — master and slave, husband and wife, parent and child. Aristotle argues that natural slavery exists: some people are fitted by nature to be ruled rather than to rule. This is the part of the Politics most modern readers will resist most strongly, and confronting it honestly is necessary to understand the limits and the strengths of everything that follows.

whyItMatters.title: Politics Begins From the Empirical
whyItMatters.body: Aristotle examined dozens of actual constitutions before writing this book. Where Plato's Republic asks what an ideal city would look like, Aristotle asks what the city is and how its real types work. The empirical approach founded political science.

whyItMatters.title: The Human as Political Animal
whyItMatters.body: The famous claim — that humans are political animals (zōon politikon) — is from this book. Aristotle's argument is that we cannot become fully human alone. The polis is not a constraint on individual freedom but the condition of its full realization.

whyItMatters.title: The Defense of the Middle Class
whyItMatters.body: Aristotle argues that the most stable regime is one with a strong middle class — neither rich enough to be oligarchic nor poor enough to be revolutionary. The argument has been rediscovered in every century since. It is recognizable in any conversation about why democracies need a broad middle.
